## Research Report: Do Increasing Childhood Vaccines Cause Autism?

**Conclusion:** The overwhelming scientific evidence does **not** support a causal link between childhood vaccines (or the number of vaccines) and autism. However, this remains a topic of public debate, partly due to recent changes on the CDC website.

### Key Evidence

**1. Origin of the claim:** The vaccine-autism hypothesis stems from a 1998 paper describing 12 children who received the MMR vaccine and later developed autism. That paper was **retracted**, and multiple large studies since have found no association. ([Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health](https://publichealth.jhu.edu/2025/vaccines-do-not-cause-autism))

**2. Large-scale studies and meta-analyses:** A 2014 meta-analysis pooling data from over **1.2 million children** found no link between any vaccine — including MMR and thimerosal-containing vaccines — and autism or autism spectrum disorder. ([PMC systematic review](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9464417/))

**3. WHO reaffirmation:** In December 2025, the WHO Global Advisory Committee on Vaccine Safety concluded that, based on available evidence, **no causal link exists** between vaccines and autism. ([WHO](https://www.who.int/news/item/11-12-2025-who-expert-group-s-new-analysis-reaffirms-there-is-no-link-between-vaccines-and-autism))

**4. Why autism rates appear to be rising:** Researchers attribute the increase in autism prevalence to **greater awareness, improved screening, and broadened diagnostic criteria** — not vaccines. Autism is also typically first identified between 12–24 months, which coincides with the vaccine schedule, creating a **temporal illusion** of causation. ([American Academy of Pediatrics](https://www.aap.org/en/news-room/fact-checked/fact-checked-vaccines-safe-and-effect-no-link-to-autism/))

### Important Context

In November 2025, the CDC revised its webpage to cast doubt on the scientific consensus, stating that studies "have not ruled out" a link. FactCheck.org and other independent reviewers have criticized this revision as **not evidence-based** and misrepresenting the existing research. ([FactCheck.org](https://www.factcheck.org/2025/11/revised-cdc-website-about-autism-and-vaccines-is-not-evidence-based/))

### Bottom Line

Your sister's claim is not supported by the bulk of scientific evidence. Decades of research involving millions of children consistently find no causal relationship between vaccines — whether MMR, thimerosal-containing, or the overall number of vaccines — and autism. The apparent rise in autism diagnoses is better explained by diagnostic and awareness factors.
